lessons.title: Freeze and Go!
objectives: Move to music and freeze when it stops

explanation: Dance is moving your body to music or rhythm. When music is fast, we can move quickly; when it is slow, we can move gently.
In freeze dance, you dance while the music plays and freeze like a statue when it stops. This helps us listen carefully and control our bodies.
Dancers move at different levels: high (on tiptoes, arms up), middle (standing normally) and low (crouching or on the floor).

story.text: At Ivaan's birthday party, they played freeze dance. When the music stopped, Ivaan froze on one leg like a flamingo, his cousin crouched like a frog, and Grandpa stood with his arms stretched like a tree. "It's a statue garden!" laughed Mama. Then the music started again and everyone wiggled and giggled.

lessons.title: Move Like an Animal
objectives: Move like different animals

explanation: Our bodies can pretend to be animals: hop like a rabbit, slither like a snake, stomp like an elephant, flutter like a butterfly.
We can also show feelings with our bodies. Happy movements may be bouncy and big. Sad movements may be slow and droopy. Angry movements may be strong and sharp.
When we put moves together, we can tell a story without any words! Many dances around the world, including Indian classical dance, tell stories this way.

lessons.title: Talking Hands
objectives: Make and name simple mudras
Show feelings with facial expressions
explanation: In Indian classical dance, hand gestures are called mudras or hastas. Each one can mean many things.

Pataka (a flat hand with fingers together) can show a flag, a cloud or a forest. Alapadma (fingers spread like an open lotus) can show a flower or the moon. Hamsasya (thumb and first finger touching) can show a swan's beak or tying a thread.
Dancers also use their eyes, eyebrows and face to show feelings — happiness, surprise, anger, fear. Hands and faces together help the audience understand the story.

vocabulary.meaning: a hand gesture in dance

examples: Using alapadma to show a blooming lotus.

lessons.title: Dances From Every State
objectives: Match folk dances to their states

explanation: Folk dances are dances of ordinary people, performed at festivals, harvests and weddings. Every region of India has its own.

In Maharashtra, the Koli dance of fishing communities shows rowing boats and waves, and Lavani is a lively dance to the beat of the dholki. In Gujarat, people dance Garba in circles during Navratri. In Punjab, Bhangra celebrates the harvest with energetic jumps.
In Assam, Bihu welcomes the new year and spring. In Rajasthan, Ghoomar is a graceful spinning dance with swirling skirts.

lessons.title: The Classical Dance Forms
objectives: Name India's classical dance forms and their states
Describe distinctive features of three forms
explanation: The Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music, dance and drama, recognises eight classical dance forms: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (North India), Kathakali (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Mohiniyattam (Kerala) and Sattriya (Assam). The Ministry of Culture also includes Chhau.

Bharatanatyam features geometric poses and strong footwork. Kathak is known for fast spins (chakkars) and rhythmic footwork with ankle bells (ghungroo). Kathakali uses elaborate green face make-up and huge costumes to act out epic stories.
Odissi features the tribhangi pose, with the body bent in three places, like temple sculptures. Each form has its own music, costume and history.

When he finally stood up in his giant skirt and crown, he wasn't a man any more — he was the hero Bhima, ready to fight for justice.

lessons.title: Dancing Around the World
objectives: Describe dances from several countries

explanation: Ballet developed in the royal courts of Italy and France and is known for pointe work (dancing on the tips of the toes), leaps and turns. French is still used for ballet steps, such as plié (bend) and jeté (jump).
Flamenco from Andalusia in Spain combines singing, guitar, handclaps and strong footwork. Samba from Brazil is a joyful dance central to Rio's Carnival.
Hula from Hawaii tells stories with hand movements and swaying hips — like Indian dance, hands carry meaning. The Chinese lion dance, performed at Lunar New Year, is believed to bring good luck.

lessons.title: Body, Energy, Space, Time
objectives: Describe dance using body, energy, space and time
Vary movements using the elements
explanation: Dance teachers often describe movement using four elements, sometimes remembered as BEST. Body: which parts move and what shapes they make. Energy: how the movement is done — sharp or smooth, strong or light.
Space: where the dancer moves — levels, directions, pathways (straight, curved, zigzag) and size (big or small). Time: tempo (fast or slow), rhythm and pauses.
Changing even one element transforms a movement. A simple walk becomes a sneaky tiptoe (light energy, low level) or a proud march (strong energy, steady time).

vocabulary.meaning: in dance, the quality or force of a movement
the path a dancer travels
the speed of movement or music

examples: A sharp, strong punch versus a smooth, light float.

lessons.title: Become a Choreographer
objectives: Create a short dance using motifs and structure
Give and receive constructive feedback
explanation: A choreographer is a person who creates dances. Choreographers often start with a motif — a short movement phrase — and develop it by repeating, reversing, changing size or speed.
Group dances can use unison (everyone doing the same move at the same time) or canon (dancers doing the same move one after another, like a round song).
Good choreographers rehearse, watch and improve. Useful feedback is specific and kind: "The canon section was clear — maybe make the ending stronger."

examples: A wave effect created by canon.

lessons.title: Abhinaya and Rasa
objectives: Distinguish nritta, nritya and natya
Explain the four kinds of abhinaya and the theory of rasa
prerequisites: Knows classical dance forms and mudras
explanation: The Natya Shastra, a Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music traditionally attributed to the sage Bharata, is commonly dated to roughly 200 BCE–200 CE. It remains the foundation of Indian performing-arts theory.

Indian dance distinguishes nritta (pure dance, rhythmic movement without meaning), nritya (expressive dance conveying meaning) and natya (dramatic performance). Abhinaya — expression — has four kinds: angika (body), vachika (speech and song), aharya (costume and make-up) and sattvika (inner emotional states).

The theory of rasa says performance aims to evoke an aesthetic emotion in the audience. The Natya Shastra lists eight rasas, including love (shringara), heroism (vira), compassion (karuna) and wonder (adbhuta); later thinkers added a ninth, peace (shanta).

vocabulary.meaning: expression in performance
the aesthetic emotion experienced by the audience
the emotion portrayed by the performer

examples: A Bharatanatyam varnam alternating nritta and nritya.

lessons.title: From Temple to Stage
objectives: Trace the history of Indian classical dance
Evaluate the 20th-century revival and its debates
explanation: Many classical forms grew in temples and royal courts. Sadir, the ancestor of Bharatanatyam, was performed by hereditary women dancers called devadasis; Kathak developed through storytellers (kathakars) and later Mughal and Rajput courts.
Under colonial rule, some Victorian-influenced reformers attacked these traditions as immoral. The Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act was passed in 1947, ending temple dedication.

In the 1930s, figures such as Rukmini Devi Arundale, who founded Kalakshetra in 1936, and E. Krishna Iyer helped revive and reshape the dance as Bharatanatyam for the concert stage. Historians debate this revival: it preserved the art but also moved it away from the hereditary communities who had sustained it, such as dancers like T. Balasaraswati, who argued for its traditional roots.

examples: Uday Shankar blending Indian and Western stagecraft in the 1930s.

story.title: Two Great Dancers
story.text: In the 1930s and 40s, two remarkable women shaped Bharatanatyam. Rukmini Devi, from a Theosophist family, brought it to new audiences and founded Kalakshetra. Balasaraswati, from a hereditary family of musicians and dancers, insisted on its deep traditional roots. Both were brilliant — and their debate still shapes how the dance is understood.

lessons.title: Training Safely
objectives: Design a safe warm-up and cool-down
Explain alignment and common injury risks
explanation: Dancers are athletes. A warm-up raises heart rate and body temperature and mobilises joints; dynamic movements are generally preferred before dancing, with static stretches more often used in cool-down.

Good alignment — for example, knees tracking over toes in a plié or the Bharatanatyam aramandi (half-sitting) position — reduces strain. Common dance injuries include ankle sprains, knee problems and overuse injuries from repetitive training.
Wellbeing matters too: adequate rest, nutrition, hydration and healthy attitudes to body image. Dance medicine and science research supports dancers' long-term health.

story.text: Meera practised aramandi for hours, letting her knees roll inwards. Soon they ached. Her teacher showed her how to turn out from the hips and keep knees over toes. With a proper warm-up and rest days, the pain faded, and her lines became cleaner. "Strong technique is safe technique," her teacher said.

lessons.title: Reading a Dance
objectives: Analyse a dance work using structured criteria
Evaluate dance's roles in identity and social change
prerequisites: Knows the elements of dance and Indian dance theory
explanation: Dance analysis considers movement (using the elements of dance), choreographic structure, music, costume, lighting and context. Like art criticism, it moves from description to interpretation to evaluation.

Dance expresses identity — national, regional, religious, gender. Choreographers such as Chandralekha (1928–2006) reimagined Bharatanatyam with yoga and martial arts to explore the body and gender; Pina Bausch's dance-theatre in Germany explored human relationships.
Dance can be political — banned, revived or used in protest — and therapeutic: dance movement therapy is used to support mental and physical health.

Some critics were shocked; others hailed a new Indian modern dance. Her work asked: what can the dancing body say today?
